questions.question: Lab 4 compares Docker images and containers to classes and objects in programming. Which statement is correct?
options: An image is like a class, and a container is like an object created from that class.
An image is like an object, and a container is like a class.
An image and a container are the same thing with two names.
A container is the blueprint, and an image is one running copy of it.
questions.explanation: An image is a reusable blueprint (like a class). A container is a running instance created from that image (like an object).

questions.question: What is a Docker **image**?
options: A process that is currently running on your laptop
A GitHub pull request that installs Docker Desktop
A lightweight, read-only template that packages what an application needs to run
A virtual machine with its own full guest operating system kernel
questions.explanation: Images are blueprints: app code, dependencies, configs, and metadata. You create containers from images.

questions.question: What is a Docker **container**?
options: Only a file sitting on Docker Hub that can never run
The Dockerfile used to describe how to build software
A Windows-only alternative to git
An isolated process (or set of processes) created from an image that you can start, stop, or delete
questions.explanation: A container is a running (or runnable) instance of an image — an isolated process on a host machine.

questions.question: Why is Docker useful for software teams?
options: It replaces the need to write application code
It packages an app with its runtime environment so it can run more consistently across machines
It automatically merges every pull request
It only helps with writing HTML and CSS
questions.explanation: Containers reduce “works on my machine” problems by shipping the app together with the environment it expects (dependencies, configs, and so on).

questions.question: How do containers differ from traditional virtual machines?
options: Containers typically share the host OS kernel and isolate processes; VMs virtualize hardware and usually run a full guest OS
Containers each run a full guest OS kernel; VMs share the host kernel
There is no difference — the terms are interchangeable
VMs are always smaller and start faster than containers
questions.explanation: Containerization isolates processes on a shared kernel. Virtual machines emulate hardware and typically boot a complete guest operating system, which is heavier.

questions.question: What does a **Dockerfile** represent?
options: A running container’s live memory dump
A list of git branches on GitHub
A recipe of steps for building an image
A password file Docker Desktop requires
questions.explanation: A Dockerfile is code that describes how to build an image — another example of treating environment setup as code.

questions.question: If you have one image, how many containers can you create from it?
options: Exactly one — images and containers are 1:1 forever
None — images cannot create containers
Only two: one for development and one for production
As many as you need; each container is a separate instance of that image
questions.explanation: Like objects from a class, many containers can be started from the same image, each with its own running state.

questions.question: When you map ports (for example, publishing container port 80 on your laptop’s port 80), what problem are you solving?
options: Copying the image from Docker Hub into git
Letting your browser on the host reach a service listening inside the container’s network namespace
Deleting unused images automatically
Turning the container into a virtual machine
questions.explanation: Containers have their own network view. Port publishing connects a host port to a container port so tools on your machine (like a browser) can talk to the app.

questions.question: By default, what happens to files written only inside a container’s writable layer if you remove that container?
options: They are typically lost with the container unless you stored them somewhere persistent (for example a volume or bind mount)
They are automatically committed back into the original image for everyone
Docker emails them to you
They permanently replace files on your host home directory
questions.explanation: Container filesystems are ephemeral by default. Persist data with volumes or bind mounts if it should outlive the container.

questions.question: What is a Docker **volume** mainly for?
options: Compiling Java source files
Naming git remotes
Storing data managed by Docker so it can persist beyond a single container’s lifetime
Blocking all network access permanently
questions.explanation: Volumes are Docker-managed storage for persistent data (databases are a common example from the getting-started tutorial).

questions.question: How is a **bind mount** different from a typical Docker volume?
options: A bind mount can only store images; a volume can only store containers
They are identical — Docker uses two names for marketing
Bind mounts only work on Windows containers
A bind mount mounts a specific path from the host filesystem into the container; a volume is storage managed by Docker
questions.explanation: Bind mounts point at a real host folder (handy in development so edits sync). Volumes are Docker-managed and are the usual choice for durable app data.

questions.question: Why run an application as multiple containers (for example, a web app container plus a database container)?
options: Because Docker forbids more than one process in any project
So each service can be isolated, scaled, and replaced independently while still working together over a network
Because images cannot include dependencies
So you never need a Dockerfile
questions.explanation: Splitting services into containers matches how real systems are composed: separate concerns, clearer boundaries, and independent lifecycles.

questions.question: What problem does **Docker Compose** address?
options: Defining and running a multi-container application (services, networks, volumes) from a single config file
Editing Python syntax errors
Replacing HTTPS with SSH for GitHub
Generating random passwords for Canvas
questions.explanation: Compose describes a whole stack in one place (often `docker-compose.yml`) so you can bring related containers up together instead of juggling many manual `docker run` commands.

questions.question: What does it mean that containers are **isolated** from each other and from the host?
options: A container cannot use any CPU or memory
Containers can never communicate over a network
Each container gets its own process space and filesystem view, so one app’s files and processes do not freely mix with another’s
Isolation means the container deletes the host OS when it stops
questions.explanation: Isolation is the point of containers: apps share the host efficiently but stay separated unless you intentionally connect them (networks, mounts, ports).

questions.question: Where do people commonly store and share public Docker images?
options: Only inside a local `.git` directory
Canvas assignment comments
The `node_modules` folder
An image registry such as Docker Hub
questions.explanation: Registries (Docker Hub is the well-known default) host images so you can pull the same blueprint onto different machines.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between building and running in Docker?
options: `docker build` creates a container; `docker run` creates an image
`docker build` creates an image from a Dockerfile; `docker run` creates a container from an image
Both commands only delete unused networks
You must run before you can build
questions.explanation: Build produces the blueprint (image). Run starts an instance of that blueprint (container).
